claims.source_section: Overview, second sentence: Antwerp engraving by Jan Sadeler I after Maerten de Vos
claims.source_excerpt: The figures derive from an engraving by Jan Sadeler I (after Maerten de Vos), published in Antwerp in 1583.
claims.visitor_claim: 18世紀のペルー・クスコで描かれたこの作品は、1583年にアントウェルペンで出版されたヤン・サーデラー1世の版画をもとにしています

claims.source_section: Overview, final sentence: birds and Cuzco landscape
claims.source_excerpt: The paradise landscape they inhabit, with its lush vegetation and brightly colored birds, is typical of Cuzco painting in the 18th century.
claims.visitor_claim: 鳥や草木に満ちた楽園の風景も、当時のクスコ絵画の特徴です

cases.source_finding: Met Overview: the figures are taken from Jan Sadeler I's 1583 engraving after Maerten de Vos; God points to the tree of knowledge; the painter uses contrasting flesh colors. Birds and plants are typical of 18th-century Cuzco painting. Same artist is unknown; do not attribute this canvas to Sadeler or de Vos.
cases.visual: The same Met 764090 official IIIF main-image (https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/api/collection/v1/iiif/764090/1954438/main-image) shows a red-cloaked gray-haired God on left pointing up toward a fruit-bearing tree; center are Eve and Adam, surrounded by dark trees and multicolored birds. The painting is not the earlier engraving.
cases.interpretation: The composition came via a 1583 print from Antwerp but the canvas was painted in 18th-century Cuzco; flora, birds, and color contrast belong to its local painted expression.
cases.emotion: The biblical warning and sacred figures substantiate modest 畏敬 strength 2; no invented feelings for Adam, Eve, God, or maker.
cases.rights: Exact work marked Public Domain by Met; its official API primary JPEG files are Open Access CC0. Modern Met prose is not reused; the Japanese explanation is newly worded.
cases.limitations: Same AI independently reread the source and Met artwork image as a separate pass, not a human expert. Unknown painter, exact print comparison beyond Met claim not independently established, and legal noninfringement is not guaranteed.

claims.source_section: Overview first paragraph: Yoshiwara oiran identified through robes and ornaments
claims.source_excerpt: The array of hair ornaments and the elaborate layers of her richly colored robes declare her to be an oiran, or a highly ranked courtesan of the Yoshiwara pleasure quarters.
claims.visitor_claim: 18世紀後半にモモカワ・シコウが描いたのは、江戸・吉原の高位の遊女である花魁です

claims.source_section: Overview: quotation of Takuan Sōhō in artist's inscription
claims.source_excerpt: The inscription by the artist quotes the Rinzai Zen monk Takuan Sōhō (1573–1645), weaving in famous Zen sayings:
claims.visitor_claim: 美術館の解説によると、絵師による上部の文章には、禅僧の沢庵宗彭の言葉や「色即是空」に通じる句が引かれています

cases.source_finding: Met overview: lavishly dressed oiran, high-ranking Yoshiwara courtesan, adjusting a pin in a double-bunned hyōgo-mage style. Upper inscription by Momokawa Shikō quotes Takuan Sōhō and Zen sayings contrasting form and emptiness.
cases.visual: Met 77180 official IIIF main image (https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/api/collection/v1/iiif/77180/2026345/main-image) shows long vertical hanging scroll, dense calligraphy above, courtesan below with elaborate dark, red, green robes; right arm raised to hair ornaments and other arm near the collar.
cases.interpretation: Text and visual combine the image of a high-ranking courtesan with Buddhist quotations. Do not infer that she herself wrote or spoke the text or that the artist condemned her.
cases.emotion: No fixed emotional response is established; no primary/secondary emotion tags claimed.
cases.rights: Met official Open Access Public Domain painting and CC0 primary JPEGs; original new Japanese explanation, not close translation of Met text.
cases.limitations: Same AI separate pass; not human expert. Exact reading of brush-written calligraphy relies on Met curatorial transcription rather than independent palaeographic interpretation. Not a legal opinion.

claims.source_section: Overview first paragraph: Johnson as earliest known professional African American painter
claims.source_excerpt: it is now accepted as an important work by Joshua Johnson, the earliest known professional African American painter.
claims.visitor_claim: 彼はアフリカ系アメリカ人として、職業画家として活動したことが知られる最初期の人物の一人です

claims.source_section: Overview opening paragraph: Edith Halpert discovery in late 1950s
claims.source_excerpt: Included in numerous international exhibitions since its discovery in the late 1950s by Edith Halpert
claims.visitor_claim: 美術館によれば、この絵は1950年代後半に画商イーディス・ハルパートによって見いだされ、その後さまざまな展覧会で紹介されました

cases.source_finding: Met Overview identifies the sitter as Emma Van Name, painted circa 1805 by Joshua Johnson. Johnson is described as the earliest known professional African American painter; artwork discovered by art dealer Edith Halpert in the late 1950s and later exhibited widely. Colors, compositional complexity and meticulous detailing make this an outstanding child portrait.
cases.visual: Official Met 701989 IIIF main-image (https://collectionapi.metmuseum.org/api/collection/v1/iiif/701989/1590752/main-image) shows young girl in lace cap and pale pink dress holding small red fruit, large glass bowl of berries at right, green drapery at right, cross pendant and patterned floor.
cases.interpretation: Portray a child and painterly choices, but do not assert the child's emotion. 'Earliest known' is a historical assessment and does not imply no other Black professional painters existed.
cases.emotion: Only secondary tentative 慈しみ strength 1, as a possible viewer response to a child's portrait; no asserted sitter emotion or creator intent.
cases.rights: Met work PD with API PD flag; original and display images are Met Open Access CC0. New original Japanese prose distinct from Met commentary.
cases.limitations: Same AI separate assessment, not an outside expert. Met API culture/classification fields are blank but official artwork page specifies Baltimore, circa 1805 and painting medium; do not infer the artwork's culture from the painter's nationality. No legal clearance guarantee.
